question_bank.question: How does the instructor characterize practical machine-learning development compared with ordinary software construction?
choices: It is mostly one-shot implementation once the architecture has been selected.
It is mostly hardware tuning because model behavior is predictable after deployment.
It is mostly data labeling because model evaluation rarely changes the next step.
It is iterative debugging because the next failure mode is hard to know in advance.
question_bank.explanation: The instructor contrasts controlled software development with ML work, where teams repeatedly discover and fix new failure modes through evidence.

source_ref.evidence_span: feels much more like debugging than development.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor stands at the front of the room while describing ML development as repeated debugging rather than a straight build.

question_bank.question: For an overnight training cadence, what daily loop does the instructor describe?
choices: Launch training, inspect results, perform error analysis, code a fix, and relaunch.
Collect labels, freeze the model, skip dev analysis, and wait for production feedback.
Read papers, change the architecture, discard the data, and restart the project.
Tune hardware, compress the model, deploy the model, and then start debugging.
question_bank.explanation: The effective cadence is evidence-driven: run training, analyze failures, implement a targeted fix, and start the next run without losing a day.

source_ref.evidence_span: You look at the results, do error analysis,

frame_evidence.description: Whiteboard shows a written daily cycle while the instructor describes morning analysis and afternoon fixes.

question_bank.question: How should a team change its workflow when training takes weeks instead of minutes or hours?
choices: Wait until the long run finishes before doing any error analysis or parallel investigation.
Stop using dev-set results because long training makes evaluation too slow to trust.
Plan asynchronous analysis and parallel experiments around the long training clock.
Replace all long training runs with smaller models even if they cannot solve the task.
question_bank.explanation: Long training jobs change the operating rhythm. Teams should launch runs, monitor them, and work asynchronously so calendar time is not wasted.

frame_evidence.description: Instructor gestures near the board while contrasting four-hour overnight jobs with multi-week training runs.

question_bank.question: Why does a slower iteration loop hurt an AI product team even if each individual experiment is technically reasonable?
choices: Slower loops force the team to use only synthetic data, so the final model cannot use real labels.
Slower loops make the architecture deterministic, so error analysis stops being useful.
Slower loops prevent the team from measuring dev-set accuracy at all.
Slower loops compound over calendar time, letting faster teams reach better systems earlier.
question_bank.explanation: Iteration speed compounds: a team that learns and fixes problems faster can reach higher performance sooner and become more competitive.

source_ref.evidence_span: they're just much less competitive in the marketplace.

frame_evidence.description: Whiteboard includes a simple performance-over-time curve while the instructor explains competitive gaps from slower iteration.
